title: Ava and the Strong Twig Bridge
markdown:
In a meadow kissed by sunshine and dotted with buttercups like fallen stars, a child named Ava sat with her kitten, Midge. Midge was a whisper of white fur, emerald eyes wide with wonder. She chased butterflies, her tiny leaps like dancing dandelion puffs. Their favourite play spot was a little toy bridge, red and blue and curved just so over a small dip in the grass.

One sunny afternoon, Midge chased a butterfly with all her might. Zip. Zoom. She landed with a tiny thump right on the toy bridge. But oh, the bridge didn’t hold firm. It wobbled and bent, dipping like a sleepy smile. Midge tumbled gently into the soft grass below, shaking her fur with a surprised little mew.

Ava, her brow furrowed, looked at the sad bent bridge. “Why did it bend so much?”

Farmer Jo, whose hands smelled of earth and sunshine, came by. “Let’s have a look,” she said, her voice as gentle as the rustling leaves.

She picked up a fallen twig from beneath the old oak tree. “Consider this. This twig is stiff. It doesn’t bend when I push it. It stays firm.”

Ava watched. The twig was indeed strong, holding its shape steady.

Then Farmer Jo found a wide smooth leaf. “And this leaf.” She pressed it gently. It curved and folded softly, not stiff like the twig.

Finally she blew on a dandelion puff, and its seeds scattered like tiny wishes on the breeze. “This is light as a feather.”

Ava’s eyes lit up, like sunbeams dancing on water. “Farmer Jo! I know! We can make a new bridge for Midge. A strong one.” She pointed to the twig. “This twig is strong for holding!”

Farmer Jo smiled. “Indeed. And what if we put the smooth leaf on top, like a little path?”

With gentle hands, they worked. They placed the sturdy twig across the dip, a firm line. Then they laid the smooth leaf over it, making a neat walkway. Midge watched, her curiosity bright.

Ava whispered, “Come on, Midge. See the new bridge.”

Midge gave a tiny brave leap.

And oh, the wonder. The twig held firm. The leaf stayed steady. The bridge did not bend. It felt solid and safe beneath Midge’s little paws. She scampered across, her tail held high, her purrs a happy vibration.

Farmer Jo knelt beside Ava. “The twig is strong because it is firm and doesn’t bend easily. It’s good for holding things up. The leaf is good for making a smooth path. By putting them together, you made a strong bridge.”

Ava looked at the twig bridge, feeling its steadiness. “So the twig is strong for holding. And the leaf is good for walking.” She giggled, a sound as light as Midge’s happy purrs.

Midge leapt onto the bridge again and again. The dandelion seeds had already blown away, too light for any path. The oak’s twig stayed where they had set it. Ava sat in the buttercups and watched her kitten cross, firm line, smooth leaf, no sleepy smile of a bend.
